summary: A framework for using transcoding services in SIP sessions, such as converting between audio codecs or between text and speech. It covers how to discover that a session needs transcoding and how to invoke it, using either a conference bridge or third-party call control. It was motivated by the needs of deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired users. This is an informational document.

eli5.summary: Two people speak different languages, so you bring in a helper who sits in the middle and translates both ways. This memo explains how phone systems find and call in such a helper.

questions: sip transcoding for deaf and hard of hearing users
conference bridge versus third-party call control transcoding
how does sip detect the need for transcoding
subtitle: How a SIP endpoint spots that a call needs a translator in the middle, and the two ways to bring one in.

tldr.problem: Two SIP endpoints may be unable to talk because they share no codec or media type, or because a user cannot use the media, for example a deaf person facing an audio stream.
tldr.mechanism: An endpoint finds out what the other side supports and then brings in a transcoding server, either with third-party call control (3pcc) or by dialing it as a two-party conference bridge.
tldr.outcome: Both models meet the transcoding requirements in RFC 3351 for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired users, and each has trade-offs in flexibility, signalling and privacy.

today: RFC 5369 is an Informational framework from October 2008, and the registry shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves the detailed 3pcc and conference bridge procedures to RFC 4117 and RFC 5370.

sections.title: The Problem and the Framework
sections.content:
Two user agents in a SIP dialog may be unable to set up a media session even when both understand the same session description format such as SDP. At the user agent level they may share no codec, or no media type (a text-only terminal and an audio-only one). At the user level, a deaf person will not understand an audio stream.

The fix is to put an intermediary that provides transcoding into the session. From the SIP point of view, introducing a transcoder works the same way for both kinds of incompatibility, and the mechanisms apply to media manipulation in general, such as a server that only raises the volume. Finding transcoding servers (media server discovery) is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If two friends cannot understand each other, you add a helper in between who changes one language into the other.

sections.title: Discovering the Need for Transcoding
sections.content:
Under the one-party consent model of RFC 3238, media manipulation services are best invoked by one of the endpoints rather than by an intermediary in the network, so an endpoint should detect the need. The offerer learns the other side's capabilities from a presence document (received in a NOTIFY request after a subscription) or from SDP: in a 200 (OK) response to an OPTIONS request, or a 488 (Not Acceptable Here) response to an INVITE.

Parallel forking can make this hard. A first attempt may reach voicemail and the next a SIP phone, and the caller cannot know which will answer; this is the Heterogeneous Error Response Forking Problem (HERFP), which this RFC leaves out of scope. The RFC recommends that an offerer not invoke transcoding before making sure the answerer lacks the needed capabilities. Wrong guesses can put two transcoders into a session that needs none. Transcoding can be symmetric (speech-to-text plus text-to-speech) or asymmetric (one-way speech-to-text for a hearing-impaired user who can talk).
sections.eli5: Before calling the helper, first check whether your friends really cannot understand each other. Otherwise you may end up with two helpers translating for nothing.

sections.title: Invoking a Transcoder
sections.content:
Once the need is found, one user agent invokes the transcoding server T, whose URI it is assumed to know. A session between user agents A and B then takes two media sessions: A to T, and T to B. The two models differ in how those are set up.

In the third-party call control (3pcc) model ([RFC4117], RFC 4117), the invoking user agent has one signalling relationship with the transcoder and another with the remote user agent, and the transcoder has none with the remote one. It suits advanced endpoints and works per stream: only streams that need transcoding go through T. It also allows different transcoders for each direction of a stream, and invoking one in mid-session is simple. Privacy is high, since T does not see the signalling between the endpoints.

In the conference bridge model ([RFC5370], RFC 5370), T acts as a B2BUA, modelled as a two-party conference server that can change the codec or the media format, for example audio to text. The invoking endpoint exchanges less signalling, which helps over low-bandwidth or high-delay links. It is less flexible: no different transcoders per stream or direction, and adding or changing a transcoder mid-session needs the remote endpoint to support the Replaces extension (RFC 3891), which the RFC says not many user agents support. Simple endpoints that cannot do 3pcc must use this model.
sections.eli5: You can either talk to the helper and your friend separately (3pcc), or ask the helper to phone both of you and relay everything (conference bridge). The first is more flexible, the second is easier for simple phones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A transcoder sees at least some of the media between the endpoints. To keep rogue transcoders out, endpoints are recommended to authenticate the transcoder, and TLS (RFC 5246) and S/MIME can be used for this.

For more privacy, endpoints using 3pcc can use one transcoder for one direction and a different one for the other, so none sees all the media. Because transcoders must read and modify media, end-to-end media security cannot be used: encryption would block access and integrity protection would block modification. Endpoints can still use media security between themselves and the transcoder.
sections.eli5: The helper hears what you say, so make sure it is a helper you trust. You can use two helpers so neither hears the whole conversation.

cells: Per stream; different transcoder per direction
